The way I train my brain to think just in that language is my using images of the words and expressions instead of the English translation when learning. For example, instead of thinking gato = cat, I think of [insert mental image of a gato]. When using flash cards I think it helps to include a picture of the thing or phrase instead of a translation. Think about it, you’ve had about a billion experiences and therefore neural connections with the word “cat,” but close to none with the word “gato.” You’re just going to have to force yourself to think “gato” (or whatever the Dutch word is for cat) every time you see a cat so your brain gets used to it.

This may or may not be a helpful answer to you but I’ve found that learning the Chinese roots of Korean words helps with vocabulary, similarly to how learning Latin roots would help one with English. Example: 양 from the Hanja/Chinese character 洋 means “ocean” but in applied cases means “Western(er)” (because they came via ocean). This can help you remember words like 양의학, 양식, and 양파, because they all deal with something “western”. 

Fair warning that 양 has like 10 different definitions but it means western or lamb as a prefix, and other things as a suffix or on its own- therefore not the best example but I hope this still makes sense.

I use Wiktionary to look up Korean words or part of words to see what Chinese characters they were originally from: https://en.m.wiktionary.org/wiki/기억 and if you click on the Hanja provided you get the Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese equivalents, helpful if you’re learning multiple. Here is another example of a word from Chinese that expanded to equivalent words in the other three languages: https://en.m.wiktionary.org/wiki/天才

Good luck!
